transcript: GTA 5 was running inside a web browser with no 100 gigabytes download, and it got taken down within hours. A site called playgta5.com loaded the full game in Chrome. Story mode and free roam both worked, reportedly even on mobile. It was unofficial and reportedly built on leaked code, so the takedown wasn't a surprise. What made it possible, though, is a completely legit tech called WASM, which is short for WebAssembly. Basically, games like GTA are written in languages like C++, which your browser can't normally run. WASM lets developers compile that code into a compact binary format the browser understands. The browser then runs it at close to native speed inside a secure sandbox. And instead of downloading the whole game first, files stream in while you play, kind of like Netflix, but for games. That's why this matters. Think about what it takes to play a game today. Boot the console, install updates, close the DLC pop-up, wait 30 minutes for a 50 gigabyte patch. With WASM, all of that becomes opening a new tab. And browser games could get even better from here. Tech like Nvidia's DLSS uses AI to render a game at a lower resolution and then upscale it so it looks sharp. Combine ideas like that with WASM, and you can imagine big games running smoothly on much lighter devices. But the question is, would you play your next big game in a browser tab? Comment below.
